query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount (up to ~10 at.%) of vanadium to the equal‐atomic NbMoTaW alloy will slightly expand the BCC lattice, lower the Peierls barrier for dislocation motion at room temperature, and thus improve ductility without undermining its high-temperature strength (at 1600 °C) or its irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal‐atomic, single‐phase BCC NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent high-temperature (1600 °C) mechanical properties, poor room-temperature ductility, and irradiation resistance predicted by first-principles calculations.
generation.intervention: Minor composition change – substitute up to ~10 at.% of one constituent with vanadium to create a modified NbMoTaW alloy.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests conducted at room temperature for ductility, at 1600 °C for high-temperature performance, and under controlled irradiation conditions to assess defect formation and damage tolerance.
generation.structural_mediator: A slight expansion of the BCC lattice and local modifications to the stacking fault energies that lower the energy barrier for dislocation movement without triggering phase decomposition.
generation.mechanism: Vanadium, being a subgroup V element with a similar atomic size, can reduce the Peierls barrier, thus enhancing dislocation mobility and plasticity at room temperature, while its low concentration preserves the high-temperature phase stability and maintains the defect-recombination characteristics critical for irradiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The vanadium-doped NbMoTaW alloys will show improved room-temperature ductility (i.e., increased plastic strain before fracture) with minimal changes in high-temperature mechanical properties at 1600 °C and unchanged irradiation resistance compared to the untreated baseline.
generation.baseline: Untreated equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy known for high-temperature mechanical performance and theoretically predicted irradiation resistance, but exhibiting very poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated only if the vanadium addition remains low (≤10 at.%) to avoid triggering secondary phases or excessive lattice distortion; the atomic size and chemical compatibility must be maintained to preserve the single-phase BCC structure and related high-temperature and irradiation properties.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in room-temperature ductility and potential minor trade-offs in high-temperature performance or irradiation behavior are uncertain and require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of NbMoTaW alloys with incremental vanadium additions (e.g., 0, 2, 5, and 10 at.%) by partially substituting one constituent (preferably one with comparable atomic size). Process all alloys under identical conditions to ensure a single-phase BCC microstructure. Conduct systematic mechanical testing at room temperature and at 1600 °C, and perform controlled in-situ irradiation experiments (e.g., using ion or neutron irradiation) to assess defect formation through microstructural analysis.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile tests to measure ductility (strain to failure) and yield strength
High-temperature mechanical tests at 1600 °C for yield strength and ductility
Irradiation experiments with subsequent TEM analysis to evaluate defect density and morphology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the vanadium-doped alloys do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility compared to the undoped NbMoTaW, or if the high-temperature strength or irradiation resistance degrades beyond acceptable margins relative to the baseline, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

However, interface weakening causes its high-temperature performance to decline at higher temperatures, severely limiting further development. In this study, a series of Al17Cr10Fe36Ni36Mo1Hfx (x = 0, 0.03, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.8 at%) alloys were prepared to study the effect of Hf content on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the matrix alloy. The results indicate that with the addition of the Hf, the Hf-rich phase began to precipitate at the interface and inside the B2 phase in the matrix alloy. In contrast, the morphology of both the FCC and B2 phases had no noticeable change. With the increase in Hf content, the high-temperature strength and ductility of the alloy first increased and then decreased, while the room temperature performance remained almost unchanged. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure. These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C,. Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm3) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added. This resulted in RHEAs with lower densities and high-temperature strengths better than the properties of Ni-based superalloys and Fe-based steels. frame.system: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW, a single‐phase BCC refractory high‐entropy alloy noted for its excellent mechanical performance at high temperature (1600 °C) and whose irradiation resistance is so far supported mainly by first-principles calculations.
frame.goal: Improve the alloy’s poor room-temperature ductility while maintaining its superior high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance.
frame.limitation: Very poor room-temperature ductility without any demonstrated experimental intervention to improve it, in contrast to its high-temperature strength and theoretically predicted irradiation resistance.
root_cause_cues: irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations
constraints: must not compromise high-temperature (1600 °C) mechanical performance
must not reduce the predicted irradiation resistance
frame.regime: Assessments need to be made at room temperature (mechanical ductility), high temperature (1600 °C mechanical performance), and under irradiation conditions.
prior_attempts: Reliance on first‐principles calculations to assess irradiation resistance has not been complemented by experimental interventions to address room-temperature ductility.
frame.understanding: A plausible mechanism is that alloying with a minor ductilizer element (for example, substituting up to ~10 atomic % of one component with a ductility‐promoting element such as vanadium) may reduce the Peierls barrier and enhance dislocation mobility at room temperature. This intervention is hypothesized to slightly expand the BCC lattice and locally modify the stacking fault energies in a way that promotes plasticity, without significantly disrupting the high-temperature phase stability or the defect‐recombination processes that underlie irradiation resistance.
frame.hypothesis: Incorporating a small amount (e.g., up to 10 at.%) of a ductility‐promoting element (such as vanadium) into the NbMoTaW alloy will create a slightly modified BCC lattice that lowers the energy barriers for dislocation motion at room temperature, thereby improving ductility. At 1600 °C, the high-temperature mechanical performance is expected to remain nearly unchanged because the added element retains phase stability and the alloy's refractory nature, while under irradiation the defect‐formation energies remain similar, preserving the resistance previously predicted by first‐principles calculations. Boundary conditions include maintaining a single-phase solid solution by keeping the doping level low and ensuring similar atomic size to limit lattice distortion. Prior evidence from related refractory high-entropy alloy systems indicates that minor additions of ductile elements can enhance room-temperature plasticity through improved dislocation mobility. A falsification experiment would involve synthesizing a series of NbMoTaW alloys with incremental additions of vanadium, then comparing their room-temperature tensile ductility, high-temperature (1600 °C) strength, and irradiation damage tolerance (through controlled irradiation experiments) against the untreated NbMoTaW baseline. If the vanadium-doped alloys do not show improved ductility or if they exhibit significant degradation in high-temperature strength or irradiation resistance, the hypothesis would be falsified.

This can improve room‐temperature ductility while minimally perturbing the high-temperature phase stability and irradiation resistance.
